title: Jesus Forgave Him Before He Healed Him
paragraphs:
Jesus Forgave Him Before He Healed Him
The paralyzed man came hoping his legs would change. Jesus looked at him and spoke to something even deeper.
Imagine hearing the roof above you begin to break.
Dust falls.
Pieces of dried mud drop onto the floor.
People start looking up.
Someone is tearing a hole through the house.

Below, the room is already packed. People are pressed against one another because Jesus is there. Mark tells us that so many gathered that there was no longer room, “not even at the door,” and Jesus was preaching the word to them.
Then four men arrive carrying a paralyzed man.
They cannot get through.
They could have gone home.
They could have said, “We tried.”
They could have blamed the crowd.
They could have promised their friend they would come back another day.
But desperate faith does strange things when it becomes convinced that Jesus is on the other side of an obstacle.
They climb.
They tear open the roof.
And then, slowly, awkwardly, perhaps frighteningly, they lower their friend into the room.
Picture the man on that mat.
Everyone can see what appears to be his most obvious problem.
His legs will not carry him.
His friends carried him instead.
He has been brought to the One whose works have already stirred entire communities.
And now he is lying in front of Jesus.
The room waits for the miracle.
Maybe the man does too.
“Stand up.”
That is what we expect Jesus to say.
But He does not say it.
Not yet.
Mark records something far more unsettling.
“When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, ‘Son, your sins are forgiven.’”
In Greek, the words are:
Τέκνον, ἀφίενταί σου αἱ ἁμαρτίαι.
Teknon, aphientai sou hai hamartiai.
“Child, your sins are forgiven.”
Stop there.
Because Jesus did.
Before He addressed the legs everyone could see, He spoke about something nobody in that room could see.
Sin.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
The deepest human problem hiding beneath the visible human crisis.
And if we rush too quickly to the moment when the man walks, we may miss the scandal of the moment when Jesus forgives.
The word Τέκνον — Teknon is tender.
“Child.”
Jesus does not begin by humiliating him.
He does not announce a catalog of the man’s sins to the room.
He does not make the broken man perform for mercy.
He addresses him with tenderness.
Then comes that extraordinary declaration:
ἀφίενταί σου αἱ ἁμαρτίαι.
“Your sins are forgiven.”
The verb comes from ἀφίημι — aphiēmi, carrying the sense of releasing, letting go, sending away, forgiving.
Think about that.
The man was physically carried into the presence of Jesus because he could not walk.
And Jesus spoke of another burden being released.
His sins.
There is something here that our generation desperately needs to hear.
We often come to God asking Him to change the thing hurting us most.
“Jesus, fix my marriage.”
“Jesus, heal my body.”
“Jesus, rescue my child.”
“Jesus, give me work.”
“Jesus, remove this anxiety.”
“Jesus, get me out of debt.”
“Jesus, make the loneliness stop.”
“Jesus, restore what I lost.”
These are not necessarily wrong prayers.
Jesus cares about human suffering.
The Gospels repeatedly show Him responding with compassion to the sick, grieving, marginalized, and desperate.
And in this very story, Jesus eventually heals the man's paralysis.
But Christ refuses to let the visible crisis convince us that the visible crisis is always the deepest crisis.
Sometimes we want Jesus to repair our circumstances while He is confronting our eternity.
We want relief.
Jesus offers reconciliation.
We want the situation changed.
Jesus wants sinners brought home to God.
We want Him to make life comfortable again.
Jesus came to make dead people alive.
And please understand what this passage does not give us permission to say.
It does not say that this man's paralysis was caused by some particular personal sin he committed.
We should never look at a disabled or sick person and casually conclude, “You must have sinned.”
Jesus Himself rejected that simplistic connection elsewhere.
When His disciples encountered a man blind from birth, they asked:
“Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?”
Jesus answered:
“Neither this man nor his parents sinned…”
That is John 9.
So Mark 2 should never become a weapon used to shame suffering people.
Jesus is doing something much greater here.
He is revealing who He is.
Because the moment Jesus declares the man's sins forgiven, some scribes sitting nearby begin reasoning in their hearts:
“Why does this man speak like that? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?”
Their theology has collided with the Man standing in front of them.
And their underlying premise contains something profoundly important.
Ultimately, forgiveness belongs to God.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly reveal God as the One who forgives His people.
Psalm 103 celebrates the LORD:
הַסֹּלֵחַ לְכָל־עֲוֹנֵכִי
ha-solēaḥ le-khol-avonekhî
“Who forgives all your iniquity.”
The scribes understand the gravity of what they have heard.
Jesus has not merely offered encouragement.
He has pronounced forgiveness.
And Mark tells us Jesus immediately knows what they are reasoning within themselves.
So He asks:
“Which is easier, to say to the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise, take up your bed and walk’?”
It is a devastating question.
Anyone can say invisible sins have been forgiven.
How would the room verify it?
But telling a visibly paralyzed man to stand up creates an immediate test.
Either he gets up…
or he does not.
Then Jesus reveals why the visible miracle is about to happen:
“But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins…”
There it is.
The healing is not merely a spectacle.
It is a sign.
Jesus turns to the paralyzed man.
“I say to you, rise, pick up your bed, and go home.”
And the impossible happens.
The man rises.
The mat that carried him into the house is now carried out by him.
Imagine that moment.
The hands that had gripped the corners of his stretcher no longer need to carry him.
The crowd that prevented him from entering now watches him leave on his own feet.
The object that once testified to his helplessness is tucked beneath his arm.
He walks out.
But never forget this:
The greatest words Jesus spoke to him were spoken before his legs moved.
“Your sins are forgiven.”
That is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because eventually every healed body dies.
Every strong body weakens.
Every beautiful face ages.
Every possession changes hands.
Every career ends.
Every earthly achievement eventually becomes somebody else's memory.
Even Lazarus, after being raised, eventually faced physical death again.
Physical healing is precious.
But physical healing is not the Gospel.
Jesus did not come merely to make our temporary lives more comfortable before the grave.
He came to save sinners.
The angel's announcement concerning Him in Matthew 1:21 was breathtakingly specific:
“You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.”
That is why the cross stands at the center of Christianity.
Our problem was deeper than bad habits.
Deeper than disappointment.
Deeper than trauma.
Deeper than financial trouble.
Deeper than physical weakness.
Humanity stood guilty before a holy God.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
Yet the Gospel does not stop at guilt.
That same passage moves immediately toward grace:
and sinners are “justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.”
This is Christianity.
Not pretending sin does not matter.
Not pretending judgment is imaginary.
Not telling wounded people to repair themselves until God becomes impressed.
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
He lived without sin.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore our sins.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose.
The forgiveness announced in that crowded house points us toward the staggering reality accomplished through Christ.
The One who had authority to say, “Your sins are forgiven,” would eventually allow nails to be driven through His hands.
The One who commanded a paralyzed man to rise would Himself rise from the grave.
The One who told that man to go home would make a way for sinners to come home to God.
That is why grace is so scandalous.
We spend years trying to hide the evidence.
Jesus already knows.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The affair you buried.
The bitterness you have learned to justify.
The secret messages.
The addiction.
The pride disguised as confidence.
The jealousy hidden beneath congratulations.
The hatred.
The lies.
The years spent performing Christianity while your heart wandered miles from Christ.
Maybe everybody thinks you are fine.
Maybe you still go to church.
Maybe you know when to raise your hands.
Maybe you can quote Scripture.
And somewhere underneath all that performance is an exhausted soul whispering:
“If people knew everything about me, would anybody still love me?”
Look again at the man on the mat.
Jesus knew more about him than anyone in that room.
And Jesus called him:
Τέκνον.
Child.
This is not permission to remain in sin.
Grace never turns rebellion into righteousness by simply renaming it.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance and faith.
But repentance is not purchasing forgiveness with enough tears.
It is not self-punishment.
It is not promising God that this time you will become worthy.
The Gospel is better.
We turn from sin and entrust ourselves to Christ because salvation is found in Him.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Maybe you have been asking Jesus to fix everything except the thing between you and God.
Maybe you have spent years praying for the circumstances around you while resisting the Lordship of Christ within you.
Maybe your prayer has been:
“Jesus, make me happy.”
And Christ is calling you deeper:
“Come to Me.”
Maybe you have been trying to walk before receiving what only grace can give.
Maybe shame has convinced you that Jesus wants nothing to do with you until you become respectable.
But look at the Gospel.
People did not clean themselves before coming to Jesus.
They came needy.
Blind.
Bleeding.
Possessed.
Diseased.
Despised.
Grieving.
Guilty.
Broken.
And sinners still come that way.
You do not crawl toward Christ carrying a résumé.
You come carrying need.
You come confessing sin.
You come empty-handed.
And the glory of the Gospel is not that broken sinners finally become impressive enough for Jesus.
The glory of the Gospel is Jesus Himself.
His righteousness.
His cross.
His blood.
His resurrection.
His mercy.
His victory.
His grace.
Maybe your “mat” is different from the man's in Mark 2.
Maybe nobody sees yours.
Maybe you have carried shame for fifteen years.
Maybe somebody hurt you and you built an entire identity around the wound.
Maybe you committed something you cannot undo.
Maybe you keep replaying a night you desperately wish you could erase.
Maybe you wonder whether God could forgive that.
The Gospel does not tell you to pretend it never happened.
The Gospel tells you something infinitely greater.
Your past does not have more saving authority than Jesus.
Your shame does not outrank His grace.
Your sin is serious enough that Christ had to die.
And His sacrifice is sufficient enough that sinners who trust Him can truly be forgiven.
That is the scandal.
That is grace.
That is why we keep saying:
He does not rewrite history by pretending evil was good.
He rewrites the sinner's future through redemption.
Peter's denial was real.
Paul's persecution of Christians was real.
The thief's guilt was real.
The Samaritan woman's broken history was real.
The prodigal's rebellion in Jesus' parable was real.
Grace does not require us to lie about the scandal.
Grace reveals that the scandal does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
And perhaps somebody reading this has been lying spiritually on a mat for years.
You have watched other people walk.
Watched other people testify.
Watched other people seem joyful.
And quietly wondered whether Jesus has forgotten you.
He has not promised that every suffering will disappear in this present life.
Christian faith does not guarantee that every believer will receive immediate physical healing, financial prosperity, restored relationships, or freedom from every earthly hardship.
Some faithful Christians carry suffering for decades.
Some die waiting for healing.
Paul himself pleaded three times for his “thorn” to depart, and God's answer was:
“My grace is sufficient for you.”
Christian hope is not built on the promise that nothing painful will happen.
It is built on Christ.
And because Christ rose, suffering does not have the final word.
Sin does not have the final word.
Death does not have the final word.
Jesus does.
One day resurrection will accomplish what temporary healing never could.
For those who belong to Christ, Revelation points toward a future in which death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, crying, nor pain anymore.
Until then, sometimes Jesus changes the circumstance.
Sometimes He gives grace to endure it.
But the sinner who comes to Christ receives something this world could never manufacture:
reconciliation with God.
If Jesus exposed everything hidden in your heart tonight…
would you run from Him?
Or finally run to Him?
There are people reading this who need to stop performing.
No more hiding behind Christian vocabulary.
No more secret agreement with sin.
No more pretending that knowing about Jesus is the same as belonging to Jesus.
Come to Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Trust the One who died and rose again.
And when you see somebody else write those words, do not become a spectator to their pain.
Pray for them.
Remind them of Christ.
We need Christian communities where confession is met with truth and grace rather than gossip.
And think about the four friends for a moment.
The paralyzed man reached Jesus because somebody was willing to carry him.
Who are you carrying?
Whose name came into your mind while reading this?
Do not merely think about them.
Send this to them.

Supporting a ministry does not purchase God's favor, prove your salvation, or make you more righteous. We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ, and financial support is one voluntary way believers can help Gospel-centered resources reach more people.
But the merchandise is not the heart of this.
Jesus is.
The mission is not building consumers.
It is helping make disciples.
It is putting biblical truth in front of exhausted Christians at midnight.
It is reaching the person quietly losing faith.
It is confronting comfortable Christianity with the Gospel.
It is reminding ashamed sinners that repentance has a destination—and His name is Jesus Christ.
And comment.
Not for an algorithm alone.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“I’m still fighting.”
“Pray for me.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
“No more hiding.”
Be honest.
Maybe this hit harder than you expected.
Because perhaps you entered this story staring at a paralyzed man's legs…
only to realize Jesus was speaking to your heart.
The crowd saw a man who could not walk.
Jesus saw a sinner who needed forgiveness.
Then Christ did what nobody in the room could do.
He dealt with both.
And centuries later, the question is no longer merely whether Jesus can make a paralyzed man stand.
Mark has already told us what happened.
The question is whether you will trust the authority of the One who told him:
“Your sins are forgiven.”
Bring Him the sin.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the years you cannot recover.
Bring Him the secret you wish you could erase.
Bring Him the exhausted faith.
Bring Him the mat.
Because the most beautiful part of your story may not be the moment everybody watches you stand.
It may be the moment, while you are still lying helpless before Christ, when you finally understand that grace came looking for you before you had anything impressive to offer.
The mat may explain how you arrived broken, but Jesus gets the final word over who you become.
